To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the addition of cAMP at high concentrations to starved cells results in a transient increase in the cytosol calcium concentration.
cAMP induces a Ca2+-influx in vegetative as well as in aggregative cells and that the cAMP-induced Ca2+ influx is mediated by the cAMP receptor.
the cytosolic calcium concentration is elevated transiently by high concentrations of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of the cytoplasmic free calcium concentration ([Ca2]i) in Dictyostelid amoebae.
a detailed characterization of the calcium signal in response to cAMP.
the study of the mechanisms that underlie the regulation of [Ca2+](i) in Dictyostelid amoebae and the role of [Ca2](i) for differentiation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cAMP-induced increase in the cytosol calcium concentration of D. discoideum is mediated by an unknown receptor, which does not require the G alpha 1 subunit of the cAMP receptor complex.
cAMP induces a transient increase in the cytosol Ca2+ concentration that is mediated by the cAMP receptor and requires extracellular Ca2+.
the increase of [Ca2+](i) in response to cAMP is mediated by the cAMP-receptor, which is coupled to a Ca2+-influx, that is independent of G alpha 2 and phosphoinositide hydrolysis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Ca2+ signal in D. discoideum cells is mediated by the cAMP receptor.

we have shown that a transient increase in the cytosol free calcium concentration ([Ca2+]) is induced in Dictyostelid amoebae when challenged with high concentrations of cAMP, and this response is dependent on extracellular calcium.

the increase in [Ca(2+)]i is mediated by a receptor coupled to a Ca(2+)-permeable ion channel, and that this receptor is not the same as the cAMP receptor involved in the induction of gene expression.
